blocks.content: Every editor has an undo button. Press it enough times and the document crawls back through every change you made, word by word, until it looks like it did an hour ago.
That behavior looks simple from the outside. Underneath, something has to remember what the document looked like at each point in time, and hand that memory back on request.

The tricky part is doing this without turning every object into an open book. The text editor should not have to expose its cursor position, its formatting runs, and its internal buffer just so some history manager can copy them out.
Memento solves exactly this problem. It lets an object save and restore its own state while keeping that state private from everyone else.
Memento captures an object's internal state in a sealed snapshot, so that state can be restored later without any other object being able to read or modify it.

The pattern shows up anywhere you need undo, redo, checkpoints, or rollback: text editors, drawing tools, game saves, database transactions, form wizards. Anywhere "go back to how things were" matters.
It belongs to the behavioral family of design patterns, alongside things like Command and Observer, because it is about how objects coordinate over time rather than how they are built or structured.
By the end of this lesson you should be able to spot when Memento fits a problem, implement it cleanly in any of a few languages, and reason about when the memory cost is worth paying.
1. Undo without breaking encapsulation
Say you are building a text editor. The core object, call it the document, holds the text, the cursor position, and maybe the selected font.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783499584894-656914823.png
blocks.alt: Document keeps private state, choosing between exposing getters and setters that leak internal fields, or creating an opaque memento handed to the history manager

blocks.content: You want an undo feature. The obvious first instinct is to have some history manager reach into the document, read its fields, and stash a copy.
Why the obvious approach hurts

["The document has to make its internal fields public, or add getters for every single one, just so the history manager can read them.","Any future field you add to the document (say, a zoom level) forces you to update the history manager too.","The history manager now understands the internal shape of the document, so the two classes are tightly coupled.","Nothing stops other code from grabbing that same internal state and mutating it in ways the document never agreed to."]
items: The document has to make its internal fields public, or add getters for every single one, just so the history manager can read them.
Any future field you add to the document (say, a zoom level) forces you to update the history manager too.
The history manager now understands the internal shape of the document, so the two classes are tightly coupled.
Nothing stops other code from grabbing that same internal state and mutating it in ways the document never agreed to.

blocks.content: You want a design where the document is the only thing that ever reads or writes its own internals. Everyone else just gets a sealed box back.

blocks.title: The core tension
blocks.content: You need to save state that lives outside the object (so it can be restored later), but you cannot let that state leak out in a form anyone can inspect or tamper with.
That sealed box is the memento. It is opaque to everyone except the object that created it.
A note on encapsulation

Encapsulation is not just about hiding fields for tidiness. It is what lets the document change its internal representation later without breaking the undo feature, or anything else that depends on it.
If the history manager depended on specific field names or types, refactoring the document would mean also refactoring the history manager. Memento removes that dependency entirely.
2. The three roles
Memento is a small pattern, just three participants, and each one has exactly one job.
Originator
The object whose state matters. It knows how to package its own state into a memento, and later knows how to unpack a memento and restore itself to that state.
Memento
A snapshot of the originator's state at one moment. It is a passive value object. It exposes nothing to the outside world except maybe a label or a timestamp for display purposes.
Caretaker

The object that holds onto mementos over time, usually in a stack or a list. It decides when to ask the originator to save, and when to hand a memento back for restoring. It never looks inside a memento.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783494827304-865015568.png
blocks.alt: Originator produces a memento, the caretaker stores it without inspecting it, and later hands it back so the originator can restore its own state

blocks.content: The caretaker is like a coat check. It hands you a ticket for your coat, and later exchanges that ticket for the coat back. It never opens the coat and inspects what is in the pockets.

blocks.title: Coat check analogy
blocks.text: The originator is the coat owner. The memento is the coat, sealed in a bag. The caretaker is the person at the counter who stores bagged coats on a rack and returns the right one when you show your ticket, never once looking inside the bag.

blocks.content: Why three roles, and not two
blocks.text: Why three roles, and not two

blocks.content: You could imagine collapsing the memento into the caretaker, letting the caretaker hold the raw state directly. That is exactly the design this pattern avoids.

Keeping the memento as its own object is what makes the state opaque. Without it, the caretaker would need direct access to the originator's fields, which is the very coupling the pattern exists to prevent.
3. Implementing the memento
The trick to keeping a memento opaque is access control, not obfuscation. Most languages give you a clean way to do this.
A narrow public surface
The memento class exposes almost nothing publicly. Only the originator, often through a private or package-level constructor, is allowed to reach in and read the saved fields.
Immutability
Once created, a memento should never change. If the caretaker or anyone else could mutate it, restoring from it would become unreliable.
Notice the memento never exposes a public setter. The only way to build one is through the originator, and the only way to read one is through a method the originator itself calls.

blocks.title: Language note
blocks.content: Java and C# often use a nested private class or a package-private constructor. JavaScript can use private class fields. Python leans on the underscore convention since true privacy is not enforced by the language.
Testing mementos
A good sanity check is a round-trip test: save a memento, mutate the originator heavily, restore from the memento, and assert the originator matches its pre-mutation state exactly.
If that round trip ever fails, either the save method is missing a field or the restore method is not writing one back, both easy mistakes to make as an originator grows more fields over time.

blocks.title: Watch for missed fields
blocks.content: The most common bug in a hand-written memento is adding a new field to the originator and forgetting to include it in both save and restore. A round-trip test catches this immediately.
4. The caretaker's job
The caretaker is deliberately dumb. It does not know what a memento contains, and it should never try to find out.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783499586958-565833283.png
blocks.alt: Caretaker holding a stack of mementos, pushing a new memento on save and popping the top one back to the originator on undo

blocks.content: What the caretaker does

["Asks the originator to save a memento at the right moments (after a meaningful change, not after every keystroke).","Stores mementos in an ordered structure, usually two stacks: one for undo history, one for redo history.","Hands a memento back to the originator when the user asks to undo or redo.","Enforces any limits, such as capping history at the last 50 snapshots."]
items: Asks the originator to save a memento at the right moments (after a meaningful change, not after every keystroke).
Stores mementos in an ordered structure, usually two stacks: one for undo history, one for redo history.
Hands a memento back to the originator when the user asks to undo or redo.
Enforces any limits, such as capping history at the last 50 snapshots.

blocks.content: What the caretaker never does
["Read fields out of a memento.","Modify a memento after it is created.","Construct a memento itself, that is the originator's job."]
items: Read fields out of a memento.
Modify a memento after it is created.
Construct a memento itself, that is the originator's job.

blocks.content: This separation is what keeps the pattern honest. The caretaker manages timing and storage. The originator owns meaning.
Multiple caretakers, one originator
Nothing stops an application from having more than one caretaker watching the same originator, say, an undo stack and a separate autosave list.
Because the originator only ever exposes save and restore, adding a second caretaker costs nothing extra on the originator's side.
5. A worked example: undo and redo in a text editor
blocks.text: 5. A worked example: undo and redo in a text editor

blocks.content: Let's wire the Editor from earlier into a full undo and redo flow using a caretaker with two stacks.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783499588783-285502010.png
blocks.alt: Editor state changes push onto the undo stack, undo pops a memento to restore previous state and pushes onto the redo stack, redo pops it back

blocks.content: The flow

["Before each edit, the caretaker asks the editor to save a memento onto the undo stack.","On undo, the caretaker pops the undo stack, restores the editor to that state, and pushes the editor's current state onto the redo stack first.","On redo, the caretaker pops the redo stack and restores that state, pushing the current one back onto the undo stack."]
items: Before each edit, the caretaker asks the editor to save a memento onto the undo stack.
On undo, the caretaker pops the undo stack, restores the editor to that state, and pushes the editor's current state onto the redo stack first.
On redo, the caretaker pops the redo stack and restores that state, pushing the current one back onto the undo stack.

blocks.content: The editor never knows a History object exists. It just answers save and restore requests. The History object never peeks inside a memento, it just moves them between two stacks.

blocks.title: Clearing redo on new edits
blocks.content: Notice recordBeforeEdit wipes the redo stack. Once the user makes a new change after undoing, the old redo branch no longer makes sense, the same rule most editors and version control tools follow.
6. The memory cost of remembering everything
blocks.text: 6. The memory cost of remembering everything

blocks.content: Every memento is a copy of state. Keep enough of them around and that adds up fast, especially if the originator's state is large.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783499590920-398357717.png
blocks.alt: Three strategies for saving state: full snapshots that are simple but large, incremental diffs that are smaller but more complex, and a capped history that bounds memory use

blocks.content: Where the cost comes from

["A naive memento copies the entire object state, even if only a tiny part changed since the last snapshot.","Long editing sessions with no cap on history can accumulate thousands of snapshots.","Deep copies of nested structures (say, a document with embedded images) are far more expensive than copying a string."]
items: A naive memento copies the entire object state, even if only a tiny part changed since the last snapshot.
Long editing sessions with no cap on history can accumulate thousands of snapshots.
Deep copies of nested structures (say, a document with embedded images) are far more expensive than copying a string.

blocks.content: Ways to keep it manageable

["Cap the undo stack at a fixed size and drop the oldest entries once it fills up.","Store diffs between states instead of full copies, and replay diffs to reconstruct a snapshot on demand.","Snapshot at coarser granularity, after a pause in typing or after a whole action, not after every keystroke.","Evict less-recent mementos to disk if memory pressure becomes a real concern."]
items: Cap the undo stack at a fixed size and drop the oldest entries once it fills up.
Store diffs between states instead of full copies, and replay diffs to reconstruct a snapshot on demand.
Snapshot at coarser granularity, after a pause in typing or after a whole action, not after every keystroke.
Evict less-recent mementos to disk if memory pressure becomes a real concern.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Strategy","Memory cost","Restore speed","Complexity"],"rows":[["Full snapshot every change","High","Fast","Low"],["Full snapshot, capped history","Medium","Fast","Low"],["Diff-based snapshots","Low","Slower, needs replay","Higher"],["Coarse-grained snapshots","Low","Fast","Medium"]]}
There is no single right answer here. A small settings object can afford full snapshots forever. A large document editor usually needs a cap or a diff strategy.

blocks.title: Measure before optimizing
blocks.content: Do not reach for diff-based mementos on day one. Start with full snapshots and a reasonable cap, then move to diffs only if profiling shows memory from history is actually a problem.
7. Why not just expose all the fields
blocks.text: 7. Why not just expose all the fields

blocks.content: It is tempting to skip the pattern entirely. Just make the document's fields public, or add getters and setters for everything, and let the history manager copy what it needs.
This works, right up until the document changes shape. Add a field, and every place that manually copies state has to be updated too, including code you may have forgotten about.

{"pros":["Memento keeps state-copying logic in exactly one place, inside the originator.","External code can never accidentally corrupt saved state, because it never gets write access to memento internals.","The originator is free to change its internal representation without breaking any caretaker code.","Multiple caretakers (undo history, autosave, checkpoints) can all reuse the same save and restore methods."],"cons":["Introduces an extra class (the memento) even for simple cases.","Naive full-state snapshots can be memory-heavy if not managed.","Some languages make true encapsulation of the memento awkward, relying on convention rather than enforcement."]}
The public-fields approach trades a small amount of short-term simplicity for long-term coupling. Memento pays a small structural cost up front to avoid that coupling entirely.
8. Real-world uses beyond text editors
Text editor undo is the classic teaching example, but the same shape of problem shows up in plenty of other systems.
Game saves

A save file is a memento of the entire game world at one point in time. The game engine is the originator, the save slot is the caretaker, and loading a save restores state without the save file needing to understand game logic.
Database transactions

A savepoint inside a transaction is conceptually a memento. The database captures enough state to roll back to that point, and the transaction manager (caretaker) decides when to roll back, without the application needing to know how rollback is implemented internally.
Multi-step form wizards
Each step forward can save a memento of the form state. Clicking "back" restores the previous step's memento instead of forcing the user to re-enter data.
Drawing and design tools
Every brush stroke or shape placement can be captured as a memento, letting a user undo one stroke at a time without the canvas exposing its raw pixel or vector buffer to a history panel.

["Game engines: save slots as sealed world-state snapshots.","Databases: savepoints and transaction rollback.","Form wizards: step-by-step state you can navigate back through.","Design tools: per-action undo for strokes, shapes, and edits.","Configuration systems: \"restore previous settings\" after a risky change."]
items: Game engines: save slots as sealed world-state snapshots.
Databases: savepoints and transaction rollback.
Form wizards: step-by-step state you can navigate back through.
Design tools: per-action undo for strokes, shapes, and edits.
Configuration systems: "restore previous settings" after a risky change.

blocks.content: 9. Memento versus Command for undo
Memento is not the only way to build undo. Command is the other common approach, and the two solve the same user-facing problem differently.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783499593361-19248623.png
blocks.alt: Command approach stores reverse logic and runs the inverse on undo, while Memento approach stores a state snapshot and restores it directly on undo

blocks.content: The Command approach
Each action is wrapped in a command object that knows how to do the action and how to undo it, usually by applying the inverse operation. Undo means calling the inverse method of the last command.
The Memento approach
Instead of reversing an action, Memento just snapshots the state before the action and restores wholesale. There is no need to compute an inverse operation.

{"headers":["Aspect","Command (inverse operations)","Memento (state snapshots)"],"rows":[["Best for","Simple, easily reversible actions","Complex state that is hard to invert"],["Memory use","Usually low, stores just the operation","Can be higher, stores full or partial state"],["Implementation effort","Needs an inverse for every action","Needs a save and restore on the originator"],["Fits naturally with","Macro recording, redo logs","Checkpoints, rollback, save and load"]]}
Some systems combine both: commands for the day-to-day undo stack, and an occasional memento as a checkpoint so a long chain of commands never has to be replayed from the very beginning.

blocks.title: Not mutually exclusive
blocks.content: Choosing Memento over Command, or the reverse, is not a permanent commitment. Plenty of production undo systems use commands for common actions and fall back to a memento snapshot for anything too complex to cleanly invert.
10. When Memento earns its keep
Reach for Memento when an object's state genuinely needs to travel back in time, undo stacks, savepoints, checkpoints in a workflow, or rollback after a failed operation.
It is not worth the ceremony for state that never needs restoring. A stateless calculator does not need a memento. A multi-step form wizard that lets users go back and forth almost certainly does.

The real signal to watch is the memory curve. If snapshots are small or infrequent, take full copies and move on. If history grows large or state is heavy, cap the stack or switch to diffs before it becomes a problem in production.

Used well, Memento gives you undo and redo, checkpoints, and safe rollback, all without ever cracking open the object whose state you are protecting. That guarantee is worth a little extra bookkeeping.
Start simple: full snapshots, a capped stack, and a clear split between originator and caretaker. Reach for diffs or coarser granularity only once real usage tells you that memory is actually tight.
